title: Jitney dance work at the Ramona with Tommy Brooks
summary: Watts rejoins Tommy Brooks's nine-piece band playing for ticket-a-dance hostesses; he explains the rotating thirty-minute breaks and the nine-to-six Saturday nights.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: I'll tell you that, I just jumped the hog, you see? Mm-hmm. You understand? I just didn't know where I was going, or who I was going to find there, but I had heard that they had two places that were colored on the street, see? And I know that if I get there and they let me give them an audition, I figure I'm going to get with one of them. That's right. You understand, see? And then I went on over there, and here, about that coincidence, there was, at the Ramona nightclub, there was my old band from St. Angelo, my old bunch of boys, Tommy Brooks.

You understand? Well, they never did get angry. We didn't have no hard feeling when I told them I want to leave and go try it in St. Angelo with Ike, you know, Benson, see? And they told me all about Ike, about what a gal he was, but I thought they was telling me a bunch of lies. But I had to acknowledge to them when I went to Hart that you told me the truth, and I wouldn't listen. And then, well, all right, Tommy, I had the job with him, see? He had an old blind trumpet player named Pearson, but he could blow a light and he could blow a lot of the trombone.
Yeah, Pearson come up there, you know he come out there and he'll go, you see?

Yeah, yeah, well, you know who I'm talking about. Yeah, he had Pearson on trumpet. He had nine pieces, see? That's strictly jitney out there, and the harps, see? A fella come in, he buy a roll of tickets, and you had twelve hostesses sitting around there. You pick which one you want, see? And every dance, you know, you'd tear off one, at least she'd tear it off, see? Well, now your music had to be kept going continuously. Now I was, was from nine to two in the weekdays. But on Saturday night, from nine, I played on many, many, many, many Saturday nights. And I saw the sun coming up way Sunday morning, and you're still feeling. That's what they tell me, that's what they tell me. Some of the girls done pull off them shoes, man, they in the stocking feet. And some of them just plain bad footed. Amen, amen. But every Saturday, from nine to five or six in the morning.

Now the way you got your break, here's the deal. One man take off at a time, take half hour. One man gets three half hour breaks, but it rotates, see? Now you got two of each, see? You got two sax, you got two trumpets. Well, I take off first, or either let Pearson go first. And when he comes back, a sax will take off. Fifteen minutes, eh? Huh? Fifteen minutes or thirty? No, thirty minutes. Oh, that was a pretty good break. Yeah, yeah, yeah. And on that long night, like Saturday night, well each man would, he would average about three breaks, see? Three, in other words, an hour and a half, see? See, but you always have to let one other man that play in that lead, he's got to be there, see? That's why, you know, two trumpets, see? I see. You know, if he go off, they don't want no sax just turning them numbers, see? I see. You played two, you played one slow when you played a medium, then you played a jump one.

In the walls. And then nothing will break the monotony, the same thing, over and over again, see? And I mean the trumpet always, he had to be the one to always pick up, he had to think, you see? He had to always, when that, alright, maybe the sax is finishing the number, maybe you done played two or three chords. If it's a short chords number, well you play three chords. If it's a long chords number, you just give the dancer two chords. And give them a three minute dance every nine days. Yeah, yeah, that's the idea. Yeah, every 30 minutes give them a three minute dance. Well now I stayed there for a year and a half for Caesar Thompson, that was the Ramona nightclub. What was it? Well they were playing 1750, see? And that was big money in them days, you know, see? Close down here is another thing. You get in them little small towns, you know, nothing but, you know, most of the people there, you know, the big shots, they're making that because it's all. That's right. But I mean there's no place to go, the theater. Yeah. And you have to drink. And I, you see, I was drinking pretty much then, you see? Yeah, a little juke joint there for us. You see? But all of us drank. Now we go to work at night, when we go to work at night, the piano player, he come there with his fifth and set it on his chair, nobody give you nothing, you buy your own.
